qs.q: A 70-year-old man presents with chronic polyarticular arthropathy affecting the wrists, second and third MCP joints, and knees, with features resembling osteoarthritis and associated carpal tunnel syndrome. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Chronic CPPD crystal arthritis can mimic rheumatoid arthritis and affects wrists, MCP joints 2 and 3, and knees, frequently leading to carpal tunnel syndrome and OA features. Rheumatoid arthritis typically has a different joint distribution pattern.

qs.q: A 34-year-old man presents with chronic wrist pain and numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers. Percussion directly over the carpal tunnel reproduces his paresthesias. What does this physical examination maneuver primarily detect?
o: Arterial insufficiency downstream from a vascular clamp
Ligamentous laxity of the nearby joint capsule
Complete functional transection of the nerve trunk
A tingling sensation produced by tapping an irritated nerve
qs.e: Tinel's sign involves eliciting a tingling sensation by tapping over an irritated or regenerating nerve to test functional recovery. It does not indicate complete nerve transection or vascular insufficiency.

qs.q: A 50-year-old woman with paresthesias in the lateral three and a half digits is evaluated for carpal tunnel syndrome. Which anatomical band forms the superficial roof of this fibro-osseous canal?
qs.e: The flexor retinaculum bridges across the carpal bones to form the roof of the carpal tunnel. The carpal bones themselves form the deep floor.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The carpal tunnel is a fibro‑osseous canal at the wrist that transmits the median nerve and nine flexor tendons. Compression of the median nerve produces characteristic sensory and motor deficits.

sections.p: A narrow passage formed by the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum. It protects structures that move the fingers while allowing them to glide smoothly.
b: Contains median nerve, flexor digitorum superficialis & profundus tendons, flexor pollicis longus tendon

sections.p: The tunnel lies on the volar side of the wrist, extending from the distal forearm (space of Parona) to the proximal palm.
b: Bound dorsally by carpal arch (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform)
Bound volarly by flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament)

sections.p: Immediately radial to the tunnel lies the thenar branch of the median nerve; ulnar to it are the ulnar nerve and artery in Guyon's canal.
b: Flexor tendons lie deep to the retinaculum
Median nerve lies superficial to the tendons

sections.p: Supplied by branches of the radial and ulnar arteries that form the superficial palmar arch and give perforating branches into the tunnel.
b: Radial artery contributes via the deep palmar branch
Ulnar artery contributes via the palmar carpal branch

sections.p: The median nerve provides sensory innervation to the lateral three‑and‑a‑half digits and motor innervation to the thenar muscles and the first two lumbricals.
b: Sensory: palmar surface of thumb, index, middle, radial half of ring finger
Motor: opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis

sections.p: Allows coordinated flexion of the fingers while protecting the median nerve from external pressure.
b: Facilitates grip and fine motor tasks
Maintains tendon glide during wrist motion

sections.p: Median nerve compression (carpal tunnel syndrome) presents with nocturnal paresthesia, thenar weakness, and positive Tinel/Phalen signs. Causes range from repetitive use to systemic disease.
b: Systemic: diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, pregnancy
Infections/tropics: HIV neuropathy, TB meningitis with wrist involvement, leprosy, chronic hepatitis B

t.b: Does tapping over the median nerve reproduce tingling? Positive indicates nerve irritation.
Does wrist flexion for 60 s cause symptoms? Positive supports compression.
Is median nerve latency prolonged? Confirms CTS; if unavailable, rely on clinical criteria.

sections.p: Look for thenar atrophy, loss of thumb opposition, and sensory loss over the lateral three‑and‑a‑half fingers. Check for associated systemic signs.
b: Sensory deficit in median nerve distribution

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive weakness leading to loss of hand function
Severe night pain unrelieved by positioning
Signs of infection (redness, fever) over the wrist

faq.q: Why does CTS worsen at night?
faq.a: Wrist flexion during sleep reduces tunnel space, increasing pressure on the median nerve.

faq.q: Can CTS be caused by pregnancy?
faq.a: Yes; fluid retention enlarges the contents of the tunnel, raising pressure.

faq.q: Is CTS always due to overuse?
faq.a: No; systemic diseases, anatomical variants, and space‑occupying lesions are common causes.
